items.followUp: Explain the changes in the diaphragm and rib cage during inhalation and exhalation.

rubric.why: Credits the mechanism of inhalation.
rubric.description: Explains how inhalation draws air into the lungs.
rubric.how: Award for describing diaphragm contraction and the resulting increase in chest volume and air entry; equivalent correct explanations are acceptable.

rubric.why: Credits the role of the rib muscles and ribs during inhalation.
rubric.description: Explains the rib-cage changes during inhalation.
rubric.how: Award for stating that external intercostal muscles contract and lift the ribs upwards and outwards.

rubric.why: Credits the mechanism of exhalation.
rubric.description: Explains how exhalation pushes air out of the lungs.
rubric.how: Award for describing diaphragm relaxation and the resulting decrease in chest volume and air leaving the lungs.

rubric.why: Credits the rib-cage changes during exhalation.
rubric.description: Explains the rib-muscle and rib changes during exhalation.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the intercostal muscles relax and the ribs move downwards and inwards.

rubric.why: Credits the pressure difference that drives airflow.
rubric.description: Relates pressure change in the chest to airflow.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that air moves from higher atmospheric pressure to lower pressure in the chest during inhalation, with the reverse during exhalation.

modelAnswer: Respiration involves inhalation, which brings air into the lungs, and exhalation, which expels air.
During inhalation, the external intercostal muscles contract and lift the ribs upwards and outwards.
The diaphragm contracts and flattens; the volume of the chest cavity increases and its pressure decreases, so air enters the lungs.
During exhalation, the intercostal muscles relax and the ribs move downwards and inwards.
The diaphragm relaxes and becomes dome-shaped; chest-cavity volume decreases and pressure rises, pushing air out of the lungs.

items.followUp: Describe how food moves from the mouth through the oesophagus to the stomach.

rubric.why: Credits the beginning of swallowing.
rubric.description: Explains how food is moved from the mouth into the pharynx.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the tongue pushes the food bolus to the back of the mouth and into the pharynx.

rubric.why: Credits protection of the airway during swallowing.
rubric.description: Explains how food is prevented from entering the windpipe.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the epiglottis closes the opening of the trachea during swallowing.

rubric.why: Credits the mechanism moving food along the oesophagus.
rubric.description: Describes peristaltic movement.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that waves of muscular contraction in the oesophagus push the food bolus forward.

rubric.why: Credits the destination of the swallowed food.
rubric.description: States that peristalsis moves food to the stomach.
rubric.how: Award for clearly stating that the bolus is propelled down the oesophagus into the stomach.

modelAnswer: During swallowing, the tongue pushes the food bolus from the mouth into the pharynx.
The epiglottis covers the opening of the trachea, preventing food from entering the windpipe.
In the oesophagus, waves of contraction and relaxation of its muscles move the bolus forward; this movement is called peristalsis.
Peristalsis carries the food bolus down the oesophagus and into the stomach.

items.followUp: Name one important book written by Jabir bin Hayan and two books written by Abdul Malik Asmai.

rubric.why: Credits a well-known biological book by Jabir bin Hayan.
rubric.description: Names a famous book by Jabir bin Hayan.
rubric.how: Award for naming Kitab-ul-Nabatat or Kitab-ul-Haywan, or giving their clear English titles.

rubric.why: Credits a well-known book by Abdul Malik Asmai.
rubric.description: Names a famous book by Abdul Malik Asmai.
rubric.how: Award for naming one of Asmai's books, such as Al-Khail, Al-Ibil or Al-Wuhush, or giving its clear English title.

modelAnswer: Jabir bin Hayan wrote Kitab-ul-Nabatat (Book of Plants) and Kitab-ul-Haywan (Book of Animals).
Abdul Malik Asmai wrote Al-Khail (Book of Horses) and Al-Ibil (Book of Camels).

items.followUp: Define biodiversity and state one reason why it varies from region to region.

rubric.why: Credits the central idea of biogeography.
rubric.description: Identifies biogeography as the study of organism distribution.
rubric.how: Award for defining it as the study of the distribution of organisms.

rubric.why: Credits the geographical scope of the definition.
rubric.description: Specifies that distribution is considered across geographical areas.
rubric.how: Award for referring to different geographical regions or areas of the Earth.

modelAnswer: Biogeography is the study of the distribution of organisms in different geographical regions of the Earth.

items.followUp: What is a parasite? Give one example of a parasite and its host.

rubric.why: Credits the relationship between a parasite and its host.
rubric.description: Defines a parasite by where it lives.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a parasite lives on or inside another organism, called its host.

rubric.why: Credits a valid example.
rubric.description: Gives an example of a parasite.
rubric.how: Award for a correct example such as tapeworm, Plasmodium, lice, roundworm or leech.

modelAnswer: A parasite is an organism that lives on or inside another organism, called its host, and obtains nourishment from it.
Examples include a tapeworm or Plasmodium.

items.followUp: What did Ronald Ross discover about the transmission of malaria?

rubric.why: Credits King's observation linking malaria with mosquitoes.
rubric.description: States the observed association between malaria and mosquitoes.
rubric.how: Award for noting that malaria was associated with places or people exposed to mosquitoes.

rubric.why: Credits King's conclusion about transmission.
rubric.description: States that mosquitoes transmit malaria.
rubric.how: Award for stating that King concluded mosquitoes spread or transmit malaria.

modelAnswer: A. F. A. King observed that malaria was common where mosquitoes were present and that people protected from mosquito bites were less likely to get it.
He concluded that mosquitoes transmit malaria from one person to another.

items.followUp: How many sodium ions and potassium ions are exchanged in one cycle of the sodium-potassium pump, and what supplies the energy?

rubric.why: Credits the correct outward movement of sodium ions.
rubric.description: States that three sodium ions are moved out of the cell.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the movement of 3 Na⁺ ions out of the cell.

rubric.why: Credits the inward movement of potassium ions and/or the energy source.
rubric.description: States the potassium movement and energy requirement.
rubric.how: Award for identifying 2 K⁺ ions moving into the cell using energy from ATP.

modelAnswer: The sodium-potassium pump uses energy from ATP to transport ions against their concentration gradients.
It pumps 3 sodium ions out of the cell and 2 potassium ions into the cell.

items.followUp: Explain how endocytosis differs from exocytosis.

rubric.why: Credits what is taken into the cell by phagocytosis.
rubric.description: Identifies phagocytosis as uptake of solid material.
rubric.how: Award for stating that phagocytosis is the engulfing of solid particles or food by a cell.

rubric.why: Credits what is taken into the cell by pinocytosis.
rubric.description: Identifies pinocytosis as uptake of liquid.
rubric.how: Award for stating that pinocytosis is the uptake of liquid or droplets of fluid by a cell.

modelAnswer: Phagocytosis is the engulfing of solid particles or food by a cell; it is sometimes called cell eating.
Pinocytosis is the uptake of liquid or droplets of fluid by a cell; it is sometimes called cell drinking.
